conversation.content:
Hello, I’m Dr. Martinez, a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers adjust emotionally after childbirth. I’ll be asking you the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS—a brief, 10-question screen that looks at how you’ve been feeling in the past seven days. It helps us pick up on any signs of depression, anxiety, or distress that can show up in the postpartum period. All of your answers stay confidential, and my goal is simply to understand how you’re doing so we can support you best. When you’re ready, we’ll go through each question together; just answer in whatever words feel comfortable. Let’s begin.

Over the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt difficult?

Honestly, laughing feels pretty hard lately. I’ll smile if someone shows me a cute video or if the baby does something funny, but it’s like the joy only lasts a second before I go back to feeling flat. My husband will joke the way he always did, and I’ll try, but mostly I just feel too tired or down to really laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things
Not really… I can force a little chuckle if someone tries hard to be funny, but it feels fake. Mostly I just feel heavy, like I’m too worn out or sad to actually laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not much… I used to get excited about little stuff—coffee with a friend, a walk, even just a quiet shower—but now it feels like nothing sounds worth the effort. I’ll plan something, then think “what’s the point?” and stay home. There are moments when I hope tomorrow might feel better, but the actual looking-forward feeling barely shows up anymore.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby won’t settle, I immediately think it’s because I’m not doing something right—like I’m missing some “mom instinct” everyone else has. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk and I sat on the nursery floor crying, telling myself I’m wasteful and careless. Even when my husband is late for work, I somehow twist it into “if I were more organized he wouldn’t rush.” I know in my head it’s not all on me, but the guilty voice keeps saying I should be better at this.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing—so I poke her foot until she stirs. I check the monitor ten times a night, convinced the room’s too hot or the swaddle’s come loose. There’s no real reason; she’s healthy, the doctor said so. But the worry just sits in my chest like a weight, and I can’t talk myself out of it for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes… it’s like a sudden wave of fear out of nowhere. I’ll be folding her tiny clothes and my chest gets tight, heart pounding, sure something awful is about to happen. I know nothing’s wrong, but I feel like I have to run and check on her anyway. It passes after a few minutes, but it keeps coming back, and each time I feel shaky and exhausted.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days I feel like I’m drowning in small stuff. She’ll cry and I’ll think, “I can’t do this,” even though I’ve done it yesterday and the day before. The dishes pile up and I stare at them like it’s a mountain. Sometimes I just sit on the couch while she naps and feel paralyzed about what to tackle next. I still manage her feeds and diapers, but everything else feels too heavy, like I’m one step away from everything crashing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yes… I’ll lie down exhausted, but my mind starts spinning—going over every little thing I might have done wrong, worrying she’ll wake up any second. Some nights I finally drift off, then jolt awake sure I heard her cry (even when she’s quiet). I probably get three or four broken hours; the rest of the time I’m just staring at the ceiling feeling sad and tense.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most of the time… I wake up with this heavy, sinking feeling that’s hard to shake. Little tasks feel huge, and I catch myself tearing up for no clear reason—like when I see other moms smiling in the park and wonder why I can’t feel that way. Some afternoons I just sit in the rocker holding her, feeling empty and weepy. I keep telling myself I should be happy, but the sadness hangs around like a fog.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s been maybe three or four times this week. Yesterday I couldn’t get her to latch, and I just broke down right there in the glider, sobbing while she cried too. Sometimes it’s smaller—spilling coffee, seeing a cute photo of someone else’s baby—and the tears just start. I feel silly afterward, but in the moment it feels like the sadness has to spill out somehow.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No… I haven’t had any thoughts like that. I feel low and overwhelmed, but hurting myself hasn’t crossed my mind.

Over the past week you've described feeling persistently heavy, joyless, and overwhelmed as a new mom. You shared that laughter feels forced, activities you once anticipated now seem pointless, and you blame yourself harshly when anything goes wrong. Daily waves of fear and nightly worry-ridden insomnia leave you exhausted, and you cry easily, wishing the sadness would lift. Despite these struggles, you continue to meet your baby's basic needs and you have not had thoughts of self-harm.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports inability to laugh genuinely and feeling too sad/worn out, aligning with "Not at all"</sym>, <sym>Response shows near-complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment and effort to engage, aligning with "Hardly at all"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive, daily self-blame across multiple scenarios, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes near-daily, intrusive, irrational worries (breathing, monitor, room temp) that persist despite reassurance, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intense panic attacks with physical symptoms (tight chest, pounding heart), recurring unpredictably and causing exhaustion—matching "Yes, quite a lot".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes feeling overwhelmed "most days," unable to handle routine tasks, and paralyzed by daily demands, matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing, self-critical thoughts and hypervigilance about the baby, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient describes pervasive sadness "most of the time," waking with heavy feelings, frequent tearfulness, and emotional emptiness matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports crying multiple times this week from sadness, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS responses map to the highest severity rating on eight of ten items, yielding a score of 26, well above the 14-point threshold indicating probable major depression. Symptoms coincide with <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: depressed mood most of the day, markedly diminished interest, excessive guilt, recurrent anxiety/panic, fatigue, and insomnia nearly every day for more than two weeks, causing clinically significant distress and functional impairment, without suicidal ideation. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent appointment with <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary-care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med>
2. Discuss starting evidence-based treatment such as <med>CBT</med> or compatible <med>antidepressant medication</med> while breastfeeding
3. Encourage 20-30 min daily outdoor walks and acceptance of household tasks left undone; ask partner/friends to help with chores and night bottle shifts
4. Practice brief breathing or grounding exercises when panic surges; place baby in safe sleep space, step away for 2-3 min if overwhelmed
5. Schedule EPDS re-screen in 2 weeks to monitor symptom trajectory and treatment response
6. Provide 24-h crisis line numbers; if any thoughts of self-harm emerge, seek emergency care immediately
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Mood/Anxiety (EPDS-based)

Symptoms/Concerns
- Marked anhedonia (Q1, Q2)
- Persistent low mood with daily tearfulness (Q8, Q9)
- Pathologic guilt/self-blame regarding parenting competence (Q3)
- Recurrent, intrusive anxiety and nocturnal panic (Q4, Q5)
- Subjective “drowning” sensation and task paralysis (Q6)
- Mood-congruent insomnia (Q7)
- Denies self-harm ideation (Q10)

Pattern
Consistent dysphoric-anxious constellation: low affect, loss of pleasure, excessive guilt, somatic anxiety, and functional overwhelm.

Screening Significance
Meets provisional elevated-risk profile for Major Depressive Episode with anxious features in postpartum context; rule-out comorbid anxiety disorder; safety screen negative for self-harm today.

Risk Factors Highlighted
- Daily sadness/crying > 2 weeks  
- Sleep disruption secondary to mood  
- Overvalued guilt / “inadequate mother” cognitions  
- Panic-equivalent episodes without medical trigger  
- Functional impairment (household tasks, social withdrawal)  
- No suicidal ideation/voices reported at present
